title: Fatigue failure in two-dimensional glasses under cyclic shear deformation
abstract: We investigate fatigue failure in two-dimensional (2D) model glasses under cyclic shear deformation using atomistic simulations. We find that the number of cycles to failure diverges as a power law as the strain amplitude approaches the fatigue limit, with an exponent close to $-1$, in contrast to the exponent of $-2$ reported in three dimensions (3D). A failure exponent of $-1$ has also recently been observed in a 2D elastoplastic model, suggesting an interesting dependence on spatial dimensionality that needs to be rationalized. Measures of accumulated plastic activity, including dissipated work and non-affine displacements, exhibit scaling with the failure time that is consistent with results in 3D, and indicate a robust connection between damage accumulation and failure. To probe the origins of the variability of failure times, we perform isoconfigurational {\it seeded} simulations in which a localized soft region is introduced. While such seeding constrains the spatial location of failure, the distribution of failure times remains broad. These findings extend recent results in 3D concerning fatigue failure times to 2D glasses, including their relation to accumulated plasticity and apparent stochasticity, while also revealing a key difference, namely the exponent describing the divergence of the failure times.
summary: This work uses atomistic simulations to study fatigue failure in 2D model glasses under cyclic shear. The key finding is a dimensionality-dependent power-law exponent for the failure time divergence (exponent $\approx -1$ in 2D vs. $-2$ in 3D). The research robustly links this failure time to the scaling of accumulated plastic damage, while also noting that failure timing remains inherently stochastic even when the failure location is controlled.
main_problem: The study investigates the phenomenon of fatigue failure in two-dimensional (2D) model glasses subjected to cyclic shear deformation.
main_result: The divergence of the failure time as the strain amplitude approaches the limit follows a power law with an exponent of approximately -1 in 2D, which contrasts with the -2 exponent found in 3D systems.
method: The research employs atomistic Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations to model the mechanical response of the glasses under cyclic loading.
model_or_system: The simulations use two specific models: the 2D Lennard-Jones (LJ) mixture potential and a 2D polydisperse soft-disk model. The system is subjected to controlled cyclic shear strain.
key_observables: Number of cycles to failure (fatigue time), accumulated dissipated work, and non-affine displacements.
important_parameters: Cyclic shear strain amplitude ($\gamma_{max}$), temperature ($T$), and the dimensionality (2D vs 3D).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the failure process is governed by the accumulation of plastic activity, and that the difference in failure exponents between 2D and 3D is due to spatial dimensionality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the power-law divergence of failure time with strain amplitude, the scaling of accumulated damage measures ($D^2_{	ext{min,init}}$ and $D_{	ext{acc}, t_f}$) with failure time, and the effect of seeding localized soft regions on failure location versus timing.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the simulation setup for 2D glasses using two models. It then analyzes the power-law scaling of failure time with strain amplitude, highlighting the dimensional difference. Finally, it correlates this failure time with the scaling of accumulated plastic damage measures, while also examining the stochastic nature of failure time variability.
why_interesting: The study provides insights into how dimensionality fundamentally alters the critical exponents governing failure in disordered materials, which has parallels in understanding phase transitions or failure mechanisms in complex quantum systems.

FIG. 2. Average failure times ⟨tf⟩against (γmax −γY max) for the (a) 2D LJ model and the (b) 2D Poly model. Solid lines are fits to a power-law which indicates that the exponent is −1, for both models. For comparison, results for the athermal quasistatic shear protocol are also shown for the 2D LJ model in (a), based on simulations reported in [29]. The distribution of failure times, for the (c) 2D LJ model and the (d) 2D Poly model, for several strain amplitudes. The distributions exhibit log-normal behaviour, with the width being proportional to the mean, as indicated by the data collapse when the axes are scaled by ⟨ln(tf)⟩.

FIG. 3. Accumulated plasticity D2 min,init (measured in terms of non-affine displacement) as a function of failure time tf for (a) 2D LJ and (b) 2D Poly. Solid lines through data represent power-law scaling D2 min,init ∼t0.4 f for both models. Dissipated work Dacc tf accumulated till failure as a function of failure time tf for (c) 2D LJ and (d) 2D Poly. A power-law Dacc tf ∼t0.8 f is observed for both the models. In (a), (c), and (d), the error bars on the exponent values represent the variation obtained by fitting different portions of the data. In (b), the line is a guide to the eye with slope 0.4.
